s1.syndrome_frame: Acute vision loss with intraocular hemorrhage and crystalline deposits
salient_findings: Spontaneous hyphema and vitreous hemorrhage in one eye
Presence of glistening crystals in the anterior chamber
Iridescent, needle-like crystals floating in the aqueous
Morning glory optic disc anomaly
Chronic retinal detachment
key_facts: Patient is a young girl
Right eye is blind
Hyphema and vitreous hemorrhage occurred spontaneously
Multiple glistening crystals were observed in the anterior chamber
Number of aqueous crystals increased as hyphema resolved
Iridescent, needle-like crystals are floating freely in the aqueous
Morning glory optic disc anomaly is present
Low-lying detachment of the peripapillary retina is observed
Chronic retinal detachment is present after vitreous hemorrhage resolution

raw.syndrome_frame: Acute vision loss with intraocular hemorrhage and crystalline deposits

Chronic retinal detachment is present after vitreous hemorrhage resolution

raw.rationale: The presence of a morning glory optic disc anomaly, low-lying detachment of the peripapillary retina, and chronic retinal detachment are characteristic features of Morning glory syndrome, which can also explain the spontaneous hyphema and vitreous hemorrhage.

rejected.label: Bietti crystalline corneoretinopathy
rejected.why: While it involves crystalline deposits, it primarily affects the cornea and retina, not typically associated with morning glory disc anomaly or the specific retinal detachments described.

rejected.label: Crystalline retinopathy
rejected.why: This condition involves crystalline deposits in the retina but does not account for the morning glory optic disc anomaly or the specific pattern of retinal detachment.

rejected.label: Cystinosis
rejected.why: Cystinosis can cause crystalline deposits in the eye, but it is a systemic disease with other prominent symptoms not mentioned in the vignette, and it doesn't specifically explain the morning glory disc anomaly or the retinal findings.

rejected.label: Hyperoxaluria
rejected.why: Hyperoxaluria can lead to oxalate crystals in the eye, but it is primarily associated with kidney stones and does not typically present with the specific ocular findings described, especially the morning glory disc anomaly.
